I see people speculating about possible motives for this, but if you've been paying attention for long enough, you know the field has a real and widespread concern about literal human extinction.

Here's the full text of a blogpost Sam wrote in 2015:

"WHY YOU SHOULD FEAR MACHINE INTELLIGENCE

Development of superhuman machine intelligence (SMI) is probably the greatest threat to the continued existence of humanity.  There are other threats that I think are more certain to happen (for example, an engineered virus with a long incubation period and a high mortality rate) but are unlikely to destroy every human in the universe in the way that SMI could.  Also, most of these other big threats are already widely feared.

It is extremely hard to put a timeframe on when this will happen (more on this later), and it certainly feels to most people working in the field that it’s still many, many years away.  But it’s also extremely hard to believe that it isn’t very likely that it will happen at some point.

SMI does not have to be the inherently evil sci-fi version to kill us all.  A more probable scenario is that it simply doesn’t care about us much either way, but in an effort to accomplish some other goal (most goals, if you think about them long enough, could make use of resources currently being used by humans) wipes us out.  Certain goals, like self-preservation, could clearly benefit from no humans.  We wash our hands not because we actively wish ill towards the bacteria and viruses on them, but because we don’t want them to get in the way of our plans.

(Incidentally, Nick Bostrom’s excellent book “Superintelligence” is the best thing I’ve seen on this topic.  It is well worth a read.)

Most machine intelligence development involves a “fitness function”—something the program tries to optimize.  At some point, someone will probably try to give a program the fitness function of “survive and reproduce”.  Even if not, it will likely be a useful subgoal of many other fitness functions.  It worked well for biological life.  Unfortunately for us, one thing I learned when I was a student in the Stanford AI lab is that programs often achieve their fitness function in unpredicted ways.

Evolution will continue forward, and if humans are no longer the most-fit species, we may go away.  In some sense, this is the system working as designed.  But as a human programmed to survive and reproduce, I feel we should fight it.

How can we survive the development of SMI?  It may not be possible.  One of my top 4 favorite explanations for the Fermi paradox is that biological intelligence always eventually creates machine intelligence, which wipes out biological life and then for some reason decides to makes itself undetectable.

It’s very hard to know how close we are to machine intelligence surpassing human intelligence.  Progression of machine intelligence is a double exponential function; human-written programs and computing power are getting better at an exponential rate, and self-learning/self-improving software will improve itself at an exponential rate.  Development progress may look relatively slow and then all of a sudden go vertical—things could get out of control very quickly (it also may be more gradual and we may barely perceive it happening).

As mentioned earlier, it is probably still somewhat far away, especially in its ability to build killer robots with no help at all from humans.  But recursive self-improvement is a powerful force, and so it’s difficult to have strong opinions about machine intelligence being ten or one hundred years away.

We also have a bad habit of changing the definition of machine intelligence when a program gets really good to claim that the problem wasn’t really that hard in the first place (chess, Jeopardy, self-driving cars, etc.).  This makes it seems like we aren’t making any progress towards it.  Admittedly, narrow machine intelligence is very different than general-purpose machine intelligence, but I still think this is a potential blindspot.

It’s hard to look at the rate or improvement in the last 40 years and think that 40 years for now we’re not going to be somewhere crazy.  40 years ago we had Pong.  Today we have virtual reality so advanced that it’s difficult to be sure if it’s virtual or real, and computers that can beat humans in most games.

Though, to be fair, in the last 40 years we have made little progress on the parts of machine intelligence that seem really hard—learning, creativity, etc.  Basic search with a lot of compute power has just worked better than expected.

One additional reason that progress towards SMI is difficult to quantify is that emergent behavior is always a challenge for intuition.  The above common criticism of current machine intelligence—that no one has produced anything close to human creativity, and that this is somehow inextricably linked with any sort of real intelligence—causes a lot of smart people to think that SMI must be very far away.

But it’s very possible that creativity and what we think of us as human intelligence are just an emergent property of a small number of algorithms operating with a lot of compute power (In fact, many respected neocortex researchers believe there is effectively one algorithm for all intelligence.  I distinctly remember my undergrad advisor saying the reason he was excited about machine intelligence again was that brain research made it seem possible there was only one algorithm computer scientists had to figure out.)

Because we don’t understand how human intelligence works in any meaningful way, it’s difficult to make strong statements about how close or far away from emulating it we really are.  We could be completely off track, or we could be one algorithm away.

Human brains don’t look all that different from chimp brains, and yet somehow produce wildly different capabilities.  We decry current machine intelligence as cheap tricks, but perhaps our own intelligence is just the emergent combination of a bunch of cheap tricks.

Many people seem to believe that SMI would be very dangerous if it were developed, but think that it’s either never going to happen or definitely very far off.   This is sloppy, dangerous thinking."

Musinsa, ClickHouse Cloud, and the New Era of AI-Powered Customer Intelligence

Musinsa’s migration to ClickHouse Cloud demonstrates how modern ecommerce companies are transforming data infrastructure into a competitive advantage.

As Korea’s largest fashion platform with 16.4 million members and thousands of partner brands, Musinsa manages enormous volumes of customer behavior data. Every click, search, cart action, and purchase creates signals that can be used to understand customers and deliver personalized experiences.

To power this capability, Musinsa built a Customer Data Platform (CDP) with an Audience Engine that allows marketers to instantly create user segments. For example, the system can identify customers who abandoned carts, specific demographic groups, or users likely to respond to certain campaigns.

However, scaling this system on self-hosted infrastructure became increasingly difficult. Storage and compute resources were tightly coupled, meaning adding computing power also required purchasing additional storage capacity. Heavy queries could impact other workloads, and maintaining the infrastructure required significant engineering effort.

The move to ClickHouse Cloud solved these limitations by separating storage and compute. Musinsa could independently scale data storage and allocate computing resources based on specific workloads. This resulted in an 86.5% reduction in storage costs and up to a 71.4% reduction in total cost of ownership.

Beyond cost savings, the architecture improved reliability. Instead of running all workloads on a single cluster, Musinsa could isolate different processes, allowing audience queries, analytics jobs, and batch operations to run independently without interfering with each other.

The company also improved real-time data ingestion by replacing external ingestion pipelines with ClickPipes. This simplified the architecture, reduced operational complexity, and allowed data to flow into ClickHouse more efficiently.

The most important development is how this infrastructure enables AI-driven marketing. Musinsa introduced MAI, an AI assistant that allows marketers to ask questions using natural language and receive analytical insights with explanations of how the results were generated.

This represents a broader industry shift. Ecommerce companies are moving beyond traditional dashboards and analytics toward AI agents that can understand customer behavior, generate insights, and automate decision-making.

The future competitive advantage will not only come from having more customers or more products. It will come from having the infrastructure to transform real-time behavioral data into intelligent actions.

Musinsa’s ClickHouse Cloud journey shows the emerging formula:

Real-time data → Customer intelligence → AI agents → Personalized experiences

Companies that build this foundation will be better positioned for the next generation of AI-powered commerce.

The emergence of procedural world generation from textual prompts, as demonstrated in applications rendering narrative environments from literary sources, highlights a significant threshold in generative modeling. This capability moves beyond static image or text creation into the synthesis of dynamic, interactive systems. Karpathy's observation of a large language model orchestrating polygonal assets in 3D space from a high-level description aligns with research in grounded language acquisition, where symbolic representations must be mapped to sensory or simulated environments.

This process can be framed within the context of "program synthesis," a field that has seen substantial progress with models like AlphaCode. However, the task here is complex, involving the translation of abstract narrative concepts ("a party of special magnificence") into concrete spatial and temporal arrangements. The "jank" or error in the output, as noted, underscores the grounding problem: the model's capacity to generate syntactically correct code for a renderer exists alongside a limited ability to "perceive" or internally validate the resulting visual-kinematic experience.

This limitation points to a core area of research in embodied AI. Work by researchers like Jitendra Malik and colleagues on learning from video and interaction suggests that models require feedback loops that are more integrated than textual or static image-based supervision. An LLM's inability to "play the game" it has created is analogous to a lack of proprioceptive or visual feedback, a challenge that work in reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF) and simulation-to-real transfer attempts to address. The potential for "ephemeral GTA of X on demand" is contingent on solving this validation and iteration cycle, likely through multimodal architectures that can process video or interactive state data as natively as they process text.
